The ending changes based on the gender of the person speaking, not the person being thanked. A man always says 'obrigado,' and a woman always says 'obrigada,' regardless of who they are talking to. This is a grammatical gender agreement with the speaker's own identity. It's a unique feature of Portuguese that English speakers often find confusing, but once you get it, you'll never mix it up again. pages.text: The most common way to say hello in Brazilian Portuguese is "oi" (pronounced "oy"). It's informal, friendly, and used all day long. For a more formal situation, you'd say "olá" (oh-LAH), and among friends, "e aí" (ee-ah-EE) is the casual go-to. Let's break down exactly when to use each. "Oi" is your default greeting in Brazil. It works in almost any casual situation: with friends, coworkers, neighbors, or in a shop. It's warm and simple, and Brazilians say it with a smile, often followed by "tudo bem?" (how's it going?). Unlike European Portuguese, where "olá" is more common, Brazilians lean heavily on "oi." If you say "olá" in Brazil, it won't be wrong, but it will sound a bit stiff, like saying "good day" in English instead of "hi." Stick with "oi" for daily interactions. "Olá" (oh-LAH) is the formal or polite version of hello. You'll hear it in business meetings, when addressing older people, or in official settings. It's not cold, just more respectful. In Brazil, "olá" is less common than "oi" in everyday speech. If you use it with friends, it might sound like you're being distant or joking. Save it for situations where you want to show respect, like talking to a boss or a stranger in a formal context. "E aí" (ee-ah-EE) literally means "and there?" but it's used like "what's up?" or "hey." It's very informal and common among friends, especially younger people. You can say just "e aí" as a greeting, or "e aí, tudo bem?" to ask how someone is. This greeting is distinctly Brazilian. In Portugal, you'd rarely hear it. If you're learning Brazilian Portuguese, using "e aí" will make you sound like a local, but only in casual settings. Avoid it in formal situations or with people you don't know. Brazilians also greet based on the time of day. "Bom dia" (good morning) is used until noon, "boa tarde" (good afternoon) from noon until evening, and "boa noite" (good night) after dark. These are polite and work in both formal and informal situations. You can combine them with "oi" for extra friendliness: "Oi, bom dia!" or "Boa tarde, tudo bem?" This is very natural. Note that "boa noite" is used both as a greeting and as a farewell, just like in English. Pronunciation is key to sounding natural. "Oi" is pronounced like the English "oy" in "boy," but shorter. "Olá" has the stress on the second syllable: oh-LAH. "E aí" is pronounced "ee-ah-EE," with a rising tone on the last syllable. In Brazil, the "r" in "tudo bem" is often pronounced like an English "h" in some regions, so it might sound like "too-doo beng" with a nasal "e." You'll hear it everywhere – at the bakery, in the office, on the phone. It's friendly, neutral, and works in any situation, formal or casual. The key to sounding natural is to use it as a greeting, not a deep inquiry. When someone asks 'Tudo bem?', they expect a quick 'Tudo bem!' back, not a detailed report. It's the Brazilian equivalent of 'How's it going?' – the answer is almost always positive. 'Tudo bom?' is just as common as 'tudo bem?' and means the same thing. article.meta_description: Learn the real ways to say 'how are you' in Brazilian Portuguese: tudo bem, tudo bom, como vai. Discover why 'tudo bem' is both question and answer.
article.h1: How Are You in Brazilian Portuguese?
article.lead: The most common way to ask 'how are you?' in Brazilian Portuguese is 'Tudo bem?' – and the answer is usually 'Tudo bem!' too. It's a greeting, not a real question about your day. Let's break down the phrases you'll actually hear in Brazil.

body: In Brazil, 'Tudo bem?' (literally 'all well?') is the standard way to ask how someone is. You'll hear it everywhere – at the bakery, in the office, on the phone. It's friendly, neutral, and works in any situation, formal or casual.

The key to sounding natural is to use it as a greeting, not a deep inquiry. When someone asks 'Tudo bem?', they expect a quick 'Tudo bem!' back, not a detailed report. It's the Brazilian equivalent of 'How's it going?' – the answer is almost always positive.
bullets: Tudo bem? – How are you? / All good?
Tudo bem! – I'm fine! / All good!
Tudo bem? Tudo bem! – The classic exchange.

body: 'Tudo bom?' is just as common as 'tudo bem?' and means the same thing. The difference is subtle: 'bom' means 'good', while 'bem' means 'well'. Both are interchangeable in everyday speech, though 'tudo bom?' might feel slightly more relaxed.

You can answer 'Tudo bom!' or 'Tudo ótimo!' (everything great). Don't overthink the choice – Brazilians use both without noticing. The important thing is to match the energy: a cheerful 'Tudo bom!' back keeps the conversation flowing.

sections.h2: Como vai? – A Slightly More Formal Option
body: 'Como vai?' (how are you going?) is another way to ask, but it's a bit more formal and less common in everyday Brazil. You might hear it from older people, in professional settings, or in songs. It's not wrong, just less casual.

If someone asks 'Como vai?', you can reply 'Vou bem, obrigado(a)' (I'm going well, thanks) or simply 'Tudo bem'. Note: 'obrigado' is used by men, 'obrigada' by women – that's a Brazilian Portuguese rule you'll want to remember.

sections.h2: Why 'Tudo Bem' Is Both Question and Answer
body: This is the beauty of Brazilian Portuguese: the same phrase works for both asking and answering. 'Tudo bem?' with a rising intonation is a question. 'Tudo bem.' with a falling intonation is a statement. You can even use it as a greeting and a farewell.
This symmetry makes it easy for beginners – you only need one phrase to handle most social interactions. Just remember to smile and say it with a friendly tone, and you'll fit right in.

body: One mistake English speakers make is translating 'how are you?' literally as 'como você está?' – which is correct but sounds stiff. Brazilians rarely say it in casual conversation. Stick to 'tudo bem?' and you'll sound more natural.

Another pitfall: don't answer with 'I'm fine' as 'Eu sou bem' – that's wrong. Use 'Estou bem' (I am well) or simply 'Tudo bem'. Also, remember that 'você' is informal in Brazil; 'tu' is used in some regions but with different verb conjugations – that's a topic for another day.

faqs.q: Is 'tudo bem' the same as 'how are you'?
faqs.a: Yes, 'tudo bem?' is the most common way to ask 'how are you?' in Brazilian Portuguese. It literally means 'all well?' and is used as a greeting. You can answer with 'tudo bem!' meaning 'I'm fine'.

faqs.q: What's the difference between 'tudo bem' and 'tudo bom'?
faqs.a: There's no real difference – both mean 'all good' and are used interchangeably. 'Tudo bem' is slightly more common, but 'tudo bom' is equally natural. You can use either to ask or answer.

faqs.q: How do you respond to 'tudo bem'?
faqs.a: The standard response is 'tudo bem!' or 'tudo bom!'. You can also say 'tudo ótimo' (everything great) or 'estou bem' (I'm well). Just keep it short and positive.

Yes, but it's less common than 'tudo bem'. 'Como vai' is a bit more formal and might sound old-fashioned to younger Brazilians. You'll still hear it, especially from older generations or in professional contexts.

faqs.q: Can I use 'tudo bem' to say goodbye?
faqs.a: Yes, you can say 'tudo bem' or 'tudo de bom' (all the best) as a farewell. It's a friendly way to end a conversation, similar to 'take care' in English.

faqs.q: Why do Brazilians answer 'tudo bem' even if they're not fine?
faqs.a: Because 'tudo bem' is a social greeting, not a real question about your well-being. Brazilians usually answer positively to keep the conversation light. If you're truly unwell, you might say 'mais ou menos' (so-so) or 'não muito bem' (not very well), but it's rare in casual greetings.
